subject: organic-chemistry-1
question: Which description correctly defines the carboxyl functional group?

options.text: A carbon atom bonded to nitrogen with no oxygen on that carbon (C—N)
A carbonyl carbon that also carries a hydroxyl group (—COOH)
A carbonyl carbon bonded to two other carbon atoms (C—CO—C)
An oxygen atom bridging two carbon-containing groups (C—O—C)

explanation:
A carboxyl group places a carbonyl (C=O) and a hydroxyl (—OH) on the same carbon, giving the condensed formula —COOH and two oxygen atoms per group. That arrangement is what makes carboxylic acids acidic (typical pKa 4 to 5), because loss of the —OH proton yields a carboxylate anion whose charge is delocalized over both oxygens. The distractors describe an amine linkage, a ketone, and an ether, none of which has an —OH bound to a carbonyl carbon and none of which is appreciably acidic.

ELI-10: A functional group is the reactive part bolted onto an otherwise unreactive carbon chain, and the carboxyl group is two parts bolted to one carbon: a double-bonded oxygen and an —OH. Neither part alone is acidic, but together the double-bonded oxygen pulls electron density away from the —OH, so that hydrogen leaves as H+ much more readily. Count the oxygens in —COOH and you get 1 + 1 = 2, which is the quickest way to tell a carboxyl from a plain alcohol on an exam structure.
